paragraphs: Friend, here's what this poem teaches me. The writer says it plain: the Lord has covered the Daughter of Zion with the cloud of His anger, and the city lies in ruins (Lamentations 2:1). He doesn't blame bad luck. He says, "The LORD has done what He planned" (Lamentations 2:17), and the children are fainting in the streets (Lamentations 2:11).

Look at where all that grief goes. The poem says, "Pour out your heart like water in the presence of the Lord." (Lamentations 2:19) Then it gives the baker actual words to pray: "Look, O LORD, and consider…" (Lamentations 2:20) The people are hurting, and they still turn toward God and not away from Him. I think that's the heart of it. Honest tears are a way of staying close to Him.

This poem isn't over when you close it, and I think that matters too. It stops in a heavy place, and it's okay to sit there a minute. But a cry like this tells you something about the One who hears it. He wants you to bring Him the whole hurt, with nothing tidied up. So next time your heart is churning, baker, take it straight to Him.
